title: How to Build a Retirement Plan That Includes Travel and Leisure
description: Budgeting for the 'Go-Go' years without running out of money.
content:
Retirement is often sold as a permanent vacation. But vacations cost money. Many retirees underestimate the cost of filling 40 hours of free time every week. The 'Go-Go' years (typically ages 65-75) often see spending *increase* relative to working years as retirees tick off bucket list items. To fund this without jeopardizing your long-term security (the 'No-Go' years), you need a 'Front-Loaded' spending plan. This guide explains how to budget for adventure.

Key Takeaways

  • The Spending 'Smile': Retirement spending is not flat. It starts high (Travel), drops in the middle (Homebody), and rises at the end (Healthcare). Plan for high withdrawals early.
  • The 'Fun Bucket': Create a separate savings account for Travel. Fund it with 'One-Time' money (bonuses, downsizing equity) rather than your monthly withdrawal baseline. When the bucket is empty, the trips stop.
  • Geo-Arbitrage: 'Slow Travel' (renting an Airbnb for a month in Portugal) is often cheaper than staying at home in the US. Travel can save money if you rent out your primary home.
  • Inflation Impact: Travel inflation (flights/hotels) is higher than core inflation. Over-budget by 10-15% for future trips.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US retirees often have high housing costs (property tax). Renting out your US home while traveling is a tax-efficient way to fund the travel. Income from your home (up to 14 days tax-free, or fully taxable rental) can cover the plane tickets.

The Travel Budget Calculator

Scenario: You want 2 big trips a year ($10k total).

Strategy A: The Permanent Withdrawal

You increase your annual withdrawal by $10k forever.
Portfolio Impact: You need an extra $250,000 in your nest egg (25x rule) to support this permanently.

Strategy B: The 'Go-Go' Sinking Fund

You only plan to travel for 10 years (Age 65-75).
Total Cost: $100,000.
Action: Set aside $100,000 in a Bond Ladder or HYSA. Spend $10k/year + interest.
Verdict: This protects your core portfolio from being drained too fast. You spend a specific pot of money to zero.

The 'Die With Zero' Approach

Prioritize experiences early when you have health. It is better to spend $10k at 65 on a trip than leave $10k to heirs at 95. The utility of money declines with age.

Tactical Tips

  1. Credit Card Hacking: Retirees have great credit and time. Opening travel cards for sign-up bonuses can pay for all your flights. It is a tax-free hobby.
  2. Off-Season Travel: You aren't tied to school holidays or work schedules. Travel in May/September ('Shoulder Season'). Costs are 40% lower.
  3. Home Exchange: Use sites like HomeExchange.com. Swap your house with someone in Paris. Lodging cost = $0.
  4. Variable Spending Rule: 'I will spend $10k on travel IF the market is up. If the market is down, I will camp locally.' Flexibility is the ultimate safety net.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does travel ruin the 4% rule?

Only if you consider it a 'Fixed' expense. If you treat it as 'Discretionary' (the first thing to cut in a crash), it fits perfectly fine.

What about travel insurance?

Essential for seniors. Medicare does not cover you outside the US. You must buy a medical evacuation policy ($200-$500) for international trips.

Should I sell my house to travel?

Some do ('RV Life' or 'Cruise Ship Retirement'). It is cheaper, but you lose the asset appreciation and a 'home base' for when health declines. Have an exit strategy.
